title: The Garden Behind the Shop
subtitle: Jasmine After Rain · Chapter 25 of 40
content:
The vine had to be moved before it climbed into the kitchen window.

Iroh called it an old medicinal variety. Mina called it a threat to the shutters. I called it the thing that had wound itself around the drainpipe in a single hot week.

"Perhaps it likes our hospitality," Iroh said.

"Perhaps it wants to eat the shop."

He considered this with insulting seriousness. "Then we must charge it rent."

We had promised ourselves an afternoon in the garden, and I had pictured a little watering and maybe tea beneath the shade cloth. Instead, the top bed had turned to mud, the jasmine leaves were yellow at their edges, and a leak in the watering line had been running since breakfast.

Lian, the neighbor whose wall bordered the garden, leaned over the low partition.

"You're watering my bricks," she said.

"We're sorry," I said.

"You said that yesterday."

"I said Iroh was sorry yesterday," I corrected. "Today I'm sorry too."

"Progress." She pointed to the dark stain spreading beneath her window. "That mortar won't stay put if it keeps getting soaked."

Iroh put down the pruning shears. He looked at the wall, then at the vine. "I have misjudged several things."

"An unusually productive afternoon," I said.

We turned off the garden tap. Mina came out with the stock book tucked under one arm, because the shop's water wasn't an endless miracle either. She showed us the weekly delivery costs. Replacing the ruined irrigation hose would mean postponing a set of decorative jars Iroh had wanted for the front shelf.

"The jars are charming," he said.

"So are walls that don't collapse," Mina answered.

Lian offered a length of spare hose from her own repairs on the condition that we return the clamp next week. I wrote the loan down. It was easier to accept a favor when it had a name and a return date, instead of becoming the sort of debt everybody felt awkward mentioning.

We dug a narrow channel to let the wet soil drain away from the shared wall. Iroh knelt in the dirt beside me. His sleeves were rolled up, his hands as practiced at pulling weeds as they had once been at something far less gentle.

"How do you know it's medicinal?" I asked, pointing at the vine.

"An old acquaintance told me."

"Did he have a name?"

"Several, depending on who was asking."

"That inspires confidence."

He plucked a leaf, frowned at its shape, and held it toward his nose. I caught his wrist.

"No tasting mystery plants."

"An outrageous accusation. I was going to smell it."

"You were absolutely going to taste it."

"Only a very small amount."

"Mina!" I called.

"Do not let him eat the plant!" she called back, without appearing.

I laughed hard enough to drop the trowel. Iroh joined in. It surprised me how good laughter could feel when the day's trouble was still sitting in plain view.

We asked a local gardener to identify the vine rather than pretending the first confident story was the correct one. It wasn't the tea herb Iroh thought it was. It could stay for shade if we pruned it, but it did not belong in any cup. Mina wrote NOT TEA on a scrap of card and tied it to the trellis.

Iroh regarded the label with wounded dignity. "It has other talents."

"So do you. I still don't put you in the kettle."

By late afternoon, the drainpipe was clear. The jasmine had been moved out of the hottest sun, the hose patched, and Lian's wall no longer glistened with fresh water. We had a list of things to check in the morning, because fixing a leak once didn't mean we could forget about it.

Mina signed off the day's stock before she went home. Iroh thanked her, and this time he did not offer to replace wages with compliments.

I carried the basin to the upper room while he washed the dirt from his hands. His knuckles were scraped from the brickwork. I reached for a clean cloth.

"May I?" I asked.

He nodded. I dabbed the worst of the scrape. His fingers curled around mine.

"You were very firm with me today," he said.

"You were trying to taste the vine."

"I was also trying to be useful."

"You were useful. Then you were wrong. You can do both."

He leaned his forehead against mine. "I am still learning to be loved by someone who argues."

"You're dating me. That's the entire experience."

A smile pulled at the corner of his mouth.

We had already talked about my other relationships, about how I prefer polyamory and honesty over exclusivity, and about the fact that affection didn't erase anybody's need for a quiet evening. I told him I was staying tonight because I wanted to, not because he had earned it by repairing a pipe.

"Then may I kiss you without submitting a maintenance report?" he asked.

"One report. In triplicate."

He kissed my fingertips first, then my mouth, slow enough that I could choose to move closer. Through the open window we could hear Mina laughing with Lian about the sign on the vine.

The shop would open in the morning. The trellis would need trimming again before long. We closed the curtains and went to bed, leaving the list where both of us could find it.
